content:
Among the many traditional Ayurvedic formulations, Triphala is one of the best-known. Its name literally refers to a combination of three fruits, traditionally used together rather than as individual herbs.

Triphala is commonly associated with digestive wellbeing, bowel regularity, and traditional rejuvenative care. However, its Ayurvedic use goes beyond simply taking it for constipation. The preparation, dosage, timing, and suitability can vary according to an individual’s constitution, digestive capacity, age, diet, and current health condition.

At Praanavaidya, Ayurvedic guidance can help determine whether Triphala is appropriate and how it may fit into an individual’s broader dietary and lifestyle approach.

What Is Triphala?

Triphala is a traditional Ayurvedic formulation made from three fruits:

  1. Amalaki (Phyllanthus emblica)
  2. Haritaki (Terminalia chebula)
  3. Bibhitaki (Terminalia bellirica)

The name “Triphala” comes from the Sanskrit words referring to three fruits.

Rather than relying on a single herb, Ayurveda traditionally combines these three ingredients to create a formulation with a broader range of properties.

Triphala is available in different forms, including:

  • Powder
  • Tablets
  • Capsules
  • Extracts
  • Traditional preparations

The form and quantity used should depend on the product and individual requirements.

Why Are Three Fruits Combined in Triphala?

The three fruits have distinct traditional roles in Ayurveda.

Amalaki

Amalaki is traditionally regarded as nourishing and rejuvenative. It is also commonly associated with digestive and antioxidant-related nutritional properties.

Haritaki

Haritaki has a long history of traditional use for digestive and bowel-related concerns. It is often associated with supporting regular elimination.

Bibhitaki

Bibhitaki is traditionally used in Ayurvedic formulations associated with digestion, respiratory wellbeing, and balancing certain Kapha-related qualities.

Together, these three ingredients form the traditional formulation known as Triphala.

Triphala and the Ayurvedic Concept of Tridosha

One reason Triphala is particularly interesting in Ayurveda is its traditional relationship with the three Doshas: Vata, Pitta, and Kapha.

Ayurvedic traditions often describe Triphala as a formulation that can be used in a balanced manner across Dosha types.

However, this does not mean that everyone should take Triphala in the same quantity or at the same frequency.

Ayurvedic assessment considers factors such as:

  • Prakriti
  • Vikriti
  • Agni
  • Age
  • Strength
  • Season
  • Diet
  • Current symptoms

Therefore, even a traditionally well-known formulation may not be appropriate for every individual at all times.

Traditional Benefits of Triphala

Triphala has traditionally been used for several aspects of wellbeing.

1. Supports Digestive Health

Digestive health is one of the most common traditional applications of Triphala.

Ayurveda places considerable importance on Agni, or digestive and metabolic function.

Triphala is traditionally used as part of approaches intended to support healthy digestion and elimination.

2. Supports Regular Bowel Movements

Triphala is particularly well known for its traditional use in maintaining bowel regularity.

It may be considered when constipation is associated with factors such as:

  • Irregular bowel habits
  • Inadequate dietary fibre
  • Poor routine
  • Sedentary lifestyle
  • Digestive irregularity

However, persistent constipation should not simply be managed with Triphala indefinitely.

Constipation can sometimes be associated with medication use, thyroid disorders, neurological conditions, bowel disorders, or other medical problems.

3. Traditionally Used for Gentle Elimination

Ayurveda traditionally considers proper elimination important for overall wellbeing.

Triphala may be used to support regular bowel function without necessarily being treated as a conventional stimulant laxative.

Its effects can vary considerably between individuals.

Taking more than necessary does not automatically produce better results and may instead cause loose stools or abdominal discomfort.

4. Supports Traditional Rejuvenative Care

Triphala is also associated with the Ayurvedic concept of Rasayana, or rejuvenative care.

In traditional practice, Rasayana approaches aim to support vitality, nourishment, resilience, and healthy ageing.

Triphala is therefore sometimes incorporated into broader wellness routines rather than being used only for digestive complaints.

5. Provides Plant-Based Compounds

The three fruits in Triphala contain naturally occurring plant compounds, including polyphenolic compounds.

These compounds have been investigated for antioxidant activity in laboratory and nutritional research.

However, laboratory findings should not automatically be interpreted as proof that Triphala prevents or treats specific diseases in humans.

Triphala and Digestive Health

Ayurveda traditionally emphasises the importance of maintaining healthy digestion.

Poor digestion may be associated with:

  • Bloating
  • Irregular bowel movements
  • Heaviness after meals
  • Reduced appetite
  • Abdominal discomfort

Triphala is traditionally used in digestive wellness routines because of the combined properties of its three fruits.

However, digestive symptoms can have many different causes.

Recurring acidity, diarrhoea, severe bloating, abdominal pain, or unexplained changes in bowel habits should be properly assessed rather than automatically attributed to “poor digestion.”

Triphala and Ayurvedic Detoxification

Triphala is sometimes marketed online as a detox supplement.

This description can be misleading.

Ayurveda has its own traditional concepts of cleansing and purification, including specialised procedures associated with Panchakarma.

Simply taking Triphala should not be equated with undergoing Panchakarma or medically “detoxifying” the body.

The body’s liver, kidneys, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and other systems already perform important physiological functions related to metabolism and elimination.

Triphala should therefore be understood within its traditional Ayurvedic context rather than promoted as a universal detox cure.

Triphala for Eye Health: What Does Ayurveda Say?

Traditional Ayurvedic literature includes Triphala in certain approaches related to eye care.

However, this does not mean that drinking Triphala can treat eye diseases.

Eye symptoms such as:

  • Sudden vision changes
  • Eye pain
  • Persistent redness
  • Flashes or floaters
  • Severe dryness
  • Loss of vision

require appropriate eye evaluation.

Triphala should not be used as a substitute for an ophthalmologist’s diagnosis or treatment.

Who Should Be Careful With Triphala?

Although Triphala is a traditional herbal formulation, it may not be appropriate for everyone.

Extra caution may be needed for people who:

  • Are pregnant or breastfeeding
  • Have persistent diarrhoea
  • Have significant digestive disorders
  • Are dehydrated
  • Take multiple prescription medicines
  • Have chronic medical conditions
  • Are preparing for surgery

People taking regular medication should discuss herbal supplements with a qualified healthcare professional because herbs may interact with medicines.

Possible Side Effects of Triphala

Triphala may be well tolerated by some people, but digestive effects can occur.

Possible problems include:

  • Loose stools
  • Diarrhoea
  • Abdominal discomfort
  • Bloating
  • Nausea

These effects may be more likely when excessive quantities are taken.

If symptoms are significant or persistent, discontinue use and seek appropriate advice.

Conclusion

Triphala is one of Ayurveda’s most recognised traditional formulations, combining Amalaki, Haritaki, and Bibhitaki into a three-fruit preparation.

Its best-known traditional applications involve digestive health, bowel regularity, elimination, and rejuvenative care. However, Triphala should not be treated as a universal remedy for constipation, weight loss, detoxification, skin problems, or other health conditions.

The way Triphala is used can vary according to an individual’s Prakriti, Vikriti, Agni, diet, lifestyle, age, and current health status.

At Praanavaidya, Ayurvedic consultation can help determine whether Triphala is appropriate for your needs and how it may fit into a personalised approach to diet, lifestyle, and traditional Ayurvedic care.

As with any herbal preparation, appropriate guidance is particularly important if you have an existing medical condition, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or take prescription medication.

Frequently Asked Questions About Triphala

What is Triphala?

Triphala is a traditional Ayurvedic formulation made from three fruits: Amalaki, Haritaki, and Bibhitaki.

What are the main benefits of Triphala?

Traditionally, Triphala is associated particularly with digestive health, bowel regularity, elimination, and rejuvenative Ayurvedic care.

Is Triphala good for constipation?

Triphala is traditionally used to support bowel regularity and may be considered for selected constipation patterns. Persistent constipation should be medically assessed rather than self-treated indefinitely.

Can Triphala be taken every day?

Some people use it regularly, but daily use is not appropriate for everyone. Individual digestion, health status, medications, and treatment goals should be considered.

Is Triphala a laxative?

Triphala may influence bowel movements, but it is a traditional multi-herb Ayurvedic formulation rather than simply a conventional laxative. Its effects can vary between individuals.

Can Triphala detox the body?

“Detox” is often used loosely in supplement marketing. Triphala should be understood as a traditional Ayurvedic formulation rather than a guaranteed body-detoxification product.

What is the best time to take Triphala?

Traditional practice often uses Triphala in the evening, but timing varies according to the individual, preparation, dosage, and intended use. Professional guidance can help determine the appropriate schedule.

Is Triphala suitable for everyone?

No. Individual factors such as age, pregnancy, digestive health, medical conditions, medications, and current symptoms should be considered before regular use.
